chapter_theme: Akananuru 61 to 80, in the anthology's order of lands: ten paalai poems of men leaving or refusing to leave for wealth, women and mothers left behind and an elopement, set beside hill trysts at night, mullai waiting and homecoming, a marutham husband held at home by his son and a courtesan's boast, and neythal pleas for open marriage. Puram fame (Pulli, Udhiyan Cheral, the Moriyar, Aay, Pittan, Paari with Kapilar, Rama at Kodi) is drawn on throughout as likeness.

61.reading: The friend tells the heroine not to waste away watching the wall where she scratches off the days since her man left for a distant land, driven by the saying that those who fall at others' hands rather than to Death are blessed; even if he won Pulli's festive Venkatam, where bowmen barter elephant tusks and drink their daily toddy, he could not stay there forgetting her breast, rich as Avi's golden Pothini.
61.nuance: The man's journey is justified with a warriors' maxim about dying in battle rather than of sickness, so a search for wealth is dressed as heroic striving; the friend answers not by disputing the maxim but by setting a famous prize (Venkatam) against a famous city (Pothini) and letting the woman's body outweigh both.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற்பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone to a far land and she counts the days

comparisons.tenor: the heroine's adorned breast and chest

62.reading: After a tryst that failed, the man tells his heart how the dark girl of their secret union, when talk broke it as loud as a war drum and meeting grew hard, yesterday clasped him to end her trembling as if she were plunging into the whirling Kaveri flood, she whose innocence is as perfect as the image the god made on the bright slopes of Poraiyan's Kolli.
62.nuance: Tonight's failure is answered with yesterday's embrace: the poem is a memory held against a broken tryst, and the closing likeness to a god-made image on Kolli sets the girl at once beyond reach and beyond blame.

colophon.thurai: அல்லகுறிப்பட்டுழித் தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret union of the hills, kept and broken by talk

comparisons.tenor: the talk that broke their union

63.reading: The foster mother tells her own daughter that she does not grieve that the girl left the great house and crossed the mountain with her lover; she grieves that her peacock-gentle child, sheltering for the night in a raiders' noisy hamlet in an old woman's rotting hut, will lie awake on his shoulder listening for the drum of cattle thieves.
63.nuance: She accepts the elopement in a single clause and spends the poem on a night she imagines in detail; at dawn on that road the red quail cock and his small hen bathe in the dust together, a pair at ease where the mother can see only danger.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் புணர்ந்துடன் செல்லச் செவிலி தன் மகளுக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone off with her lover across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the girl's soft gait and innocence

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the foster mother's own daughter is the heroine's friend (நின் தோழி, line 1)

64.reading: Returning with his task done, the man urges his charioteer through the wet red country of the rains: at this hour the bull with earth on its horns leads the young heifer home and the cows' clear bells fill the village common, and she who waits for him is undone each time she hears them in the lonely evening.
64.nuance: The sound that marks every other homecoming (the cows' bells at dusk) is the sound that torments her, so his haste is set against a sound she hears without him.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளும் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: rain season and evening, with a herd coming home

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the plumed horses

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாக, line 1)

iraicchi.act: the bull, wanting to be together, takes the young heifer close and heads home to the village
iraicchi.sense: the man's own homecoming is this one, and he hurries so that she is not left alone at the hour when even the herd is paired

65.reading: The friend tells the heroine to rejoice like the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral, for they are free of the suspicious mother and the lying women of the street: the man has today set out with them on the very journey he once put off, saying the hard road over the hills, lit with bamboo fires like fishing boats' lamps at sea and guarded by a tusker, was too hard for women.
65.nuance: The friend quotes his old refusal in full, the road's beauty and danger included, so the elopement is told as his change of mind; the bards' joy before a famous giver is the measure of the girls' release.

colophon.thurai: வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தலைமகன் உடன்போக்கு வலித்தமை தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers set out together across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the girls' joy at going with him
the fires bamboo friction kindles on the hills

66.reading: The heroine tells the friend who came on her husband's behalf that the old saying (sons bring fame here and a clean passage hereafter) has proved true: yesterday, dressed to wed another, he stopped his chariot when their little son ran out to see him, could not hand the crying boy back, came into the house with him, and, held by the memory of the kindness he once showed her among the girls at play, gave up the wedding though its drums kept calling him.
66.nuance: The proverb about sons is a puram commonplace about fame and the next world; she tests it on a household quarrel and finds it true in a way the proverb never meant, since the son's merit is that he keeps his father at home. Her own part is comic and rueful: ashamed to seem the cause, she makes a show of beating the boy.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தையிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகற்கு வாயிலாய்ப்புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband sets out to marry another woman

comparisons.tenor: the boy who stops his father
the wedding drums seeming to call him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend has come as the husband's go-between

67.reading: The heroine asks her friend what she can do, when they say the road her man took is a rainless gravel waste where marauders rush at night, hero-stones crowned with peacock feathers stand like a battle front, stone heaps mark where men fell, and the gravel glitters like fireflies beside a ghost's mirage.
67.nuance: Everything she describes is hearsay (என்ப): the dread comes from report, and the poem's last line puts the road beside the beauty he gave up to travel it.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தவழி வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cloud withholds its rain from a gravel upland

comparisons.tenor: the hero-stones with spears planted and shields set
the stone heaps over the fallen

68.reading: The friend tells the heroine how, testing whether their mother slept, she asked her whether she had heard the waterfall shaking the koothalam and the thunder that split the asoka where their swing hangs; the mother, hearing nothing, sank into sleep, all creatures slept, and the man, as their hearts had hoped, came through the cold road of torrents, crying elephants and pythons.
68.nuance: The friend's innocent-sounding questions are a sleep test, and the noise of the night (falls, thunder, flood) is both the cover for his coming and the danger he braved to come.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இரவுக்குறி வந்தமையறிந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover comes by night while the house sleeps

comparisons.tenor: the swing's rope, struck as if it were a snake

69.reading: The friend tells the heroine, wasted and dimmed in eye and colour, to stop weeping: though the man, wanting the joy of giving, has gone past the rock the Moriyar's chariot wheels cut, through summer wastes where deer herds strip the nelli, he will not stay long forgetting sweet sleep on her breast, fragrant as the first-day blossom of Aay's forest.
69.nuance: The friend grants his motive full dignity (he went for wealth to give, ஈதல் இன்பம்), and uses that dignity as her argument: a man moved by giving will not hoard his absence.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து நீட்டித்தான் தலைமகன் எனக் கவன்ற தலைமகட்கு வருவரென்பதுபடச் சொல்லித் தோழி ஆற்றுவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to earn wealth

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which have lost the dark flower's loveliness

70.reading: The friend tells the heroine that their love for the lord of the fishing shore, once broadcast by gossiping women, is now crowned by the wedding, and the noisy town has fallen silent, like the banyan whose birds Rama, victor in war, hushed for his secret counsel at the ancient Kodi of the Kavuriyar.
70.nuance: Gossip, the force that drives so many akam poems, is here simply shut off by marriage; the Rama legend supplies the image of a silence imposed on a whole clamorous tree.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைவு மலிந்தமை தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: fishers, the neythal flower and the shore grove

71.reading: In the evening that ends the day, when bees leave pool flowers for branch flowers like graceless men who drop the poor, deer stand bewildered and the sky blooms like cooling gold, the speaker tells her friend that the evening's pain strikes like spearmen aiming at a wounded man's vital spot, her strength thins like breath in a furnace, and asks if this is the hour her life will leave her like a bird quitting a tree in a gale.
71.nuance: The opening simile is about bees, but its vehicle (men who leave those who are no longer useful) falls on the absent lover without naming him.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த விடத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது,

thinai_evidence.note: the pain of a lover gone

comparisons.tenor: the bees leaving pool flowers for branch flowers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives the friend as speaker, but the poem speaks of என் உயிர் and addresses the friend

72.reading: With the man standing outside at the night tryst, the heroine tells her friend that the road he came by at midnight in the rain is fearful (lightning on the anthills where a bear digs, rivers with crocodiles, a tiger that killed an elephant for its pregnant mate, paths like walking a sword's edge), and that he who came with a loving heart and only a spear for company is not cruel, nor is the friend who brought him at fault: the fault is hers.
72.nuance: Spoken for his ears, the self-blame is a plea: by listing the road's terrors and taking the guilt on herself she tells him the night visits must end in marriage.

colophon.thurai: (1) தலைமகன் இரவுக்குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover comes at midnight through the hills

comparisons.tenor: the bear digging in the glowing anthill

iraicchi.act: the tiger kills a great elephant to end the craving hunger of his pregnant mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who braves such a road at night does it out of the same care for her, so he is not cruel

73.reading: One woman calls to the other (the colophon implies the friend speaks; the poem addresses the friend) that, since their pain is one, they should go and see what is coming to end it: over the land where he went the rain cloud stands, flashing like the sparks from a millet-guard's brand.
73.nuance: The rain cloud is both comfort and accusation: it is the season he named for his return, seen over his country, not yet over hers.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிகின்றான். குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு அழிந்த தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the promised rains are seen arriving

comparisons.tenor: the gleam of the single pearl string

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the poem's own address to காதல்அம் தோழி and its 'my ruin' suggest the heroine speaks to the friend

74.reading: The heroine tells the friend who keeps assuring her that the man, his task won, will see the startled doe of the stag in the rain-washed scrub, think of her and order his charioteer to hurry, that she could hold firm on that comfort if only the cowherds' small harsh flute did not torment her in the evening.
74.nuance: Almost the whole poem is the friend's comfort, quoted back; the last three lines undo it with a single sound of her own mullai land.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் அழிந்த கிழத்தி வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai flowers, cowherds and their flute

comparisons.tenor: the red mites on the road
her own startled eyes, which he will recall

75.reading: Answering the woman's fear that he will leave, the man recalls the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth, says that those who follow it across burnt hills only grieve ever after for beauty that wasted unembraced and that no one in this world can give back, and asks whether he could ever plan to leave her, so hard a prize to win.
75.nuance: The opening maxim is quoted to be refuted, and the refutation turns on a pun: the vision that decided on wealth is பொருள்அல் காட்சி, a view that misses the point (பொருள்) even as it pursues wealth (பொருள்).

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிவரென வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குப் பிரியேனெனத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: parting for wealth is debated and refused

76.reading: Told that the wife's people rail at her, the courtesan says within their hearing that his women may keep on clamouring like bards' drums at a patron's morning feast; as Aathi Manthi wandered distraught asking who had seen her curly-haired dancer and the cool Kaveri held him, so she has resolved to seize the man and hold him fast.
76.nuance: The courtesan borrows the Aathi Manthi legend and takes the river's part in it, leaving the wife the role of the bereaved queen.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளை நயப்பித்துக் கொண்டாளென்று கழறக்கேட்ட பரத்தை தலைமகள் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the ford town visits the courtesans' street

comparisons.tenor: her seizing and holding the man

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: spoken so that the heroine's companions (பாங்காயினார்) hear

77.reading: The man tells his heart that if it plots to cross the forest for wealth though her brow pale, it plots ill: past ruined villages where vultures pull out the guts of fallen warriors, at the dark evening in a hamlet's ithi shade, her tear-filled eyes will wound him like the spear Pittan, Chera's generous warrior, raised against hostile kings.
77.nuance: The parting is stopped in the imagination: the man pictures the evening of the journey, and what decides is not the road's danger but her eyes as he will remember them.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரியக் கருதிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லி, செலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighs leaving her to earn wealth

comparisons.tenor: the vulture pulling out the guts of the dead

78.reading: The friend asks the hill-lord, back from his absence, whether in his few days away he ever once thought of them in the cold dewy season, when the tusker on the slope, afraid of the yali, wraps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk; and she says the girl's brow smells of the new flowers of Paari's pool, Paari who with Kapilar beside him held out for years and drove the kings away.
78.nuance: The friend puts the right thought into his mouth (how will they fare, poor things, alone in our town?) and then asks if he ever had it; the brow fragrant as Paari's pool makes the girl a prize kings could not take.

colophon.thurai: களவுக் காலத்துப் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: hill folk, kaanthal and the mountain slope

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the girl's brow

iraicchi.act: the tusker, fearing the yali, clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk to shelter her
iraicchi.sense: the man should guard the girl who trembles alone through the cold season, as the beast of his own hill guards his mate, instead of leaving her

79.reading: Midway across the waste, the man tells his heart that it has suffered for wealth that never stays, crossing the hard ground of stone-cut wells, the red dust of the Kongar herds rushing to water, and the long road where the kite's mate calls while the Eyinar bowmen go out raiding to their drum.
79.nuance: The last word is the charge: the wealth that drew him is நில்லாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, so the hardship is spent on something already slipping away.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் இடைச் சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her, bound by the desire for wealth

80.reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool shore that he has truly come by night, swimming the dark backwater where crocodiles and sharks move; asking whether they are so hard for him to reach, she says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish, and bids him drive his chariot over the adumbu creepers and come by day to the punnai grove.
80.nuance: The invitation by day is a refusal of the night: a chariot that cuts the shore creepers leaves a track everyone can see, so the friend is asking for a courtship in the open.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிவந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: crocodiles of the backwater and the punnai grove of the shore

links.note: Purananuru 93 describes the rite of cutting with a sword the body of a king who died of sickness, so that he goes where battle-slain warriors go; Akananuru 61 opens with the saying behind that rite (blessed are those who die at others' hands, not seized by Death) as the reason a man leaves home.
links.teaches: Together they show the warrior's creed about a good death working at two scales: as a royal funeral rite in puram, and in akam as a proverb that sends an ordinary man away from his wife to strive.

links.note: Both are the friend's comfort in paalai: in 61 even winning Pulli's Venkatam will not keep him, in 209 even going beyond Pulli's Venkatam he will not forget; both close by likening the heroine's beauty to a famous place (Pothini, the Kolli image).
links.teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served the paalai poets as the fixed northern limit of a man's absence, so different poets could promise his return by measuring it against the same frontier and the same kind of famous-place likeness.

links.note: Paranar in 62 and Kalladanar in 209 both liken the heroine to the image on Kolli that a god made: one in the lover's own memory after a failed tryst, the other in the friend's comfort during his absence.
links.teaches: The Kolli image was a shared likeness for a beauty that cannot be harmed or taken, used by a kurinji lover and a paalai friend alike, so the legend of the hill carried a fixed sense of untouchable loveliness.

links.note: Both are the returning man's words to his charioteer in mullai, and both set a pair of beasts going together (the stag and doe in 34, the bull and heifer in 64) beside his haste; 64 adds the cows' evening bells, which the wife hears alone.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the iraicchi tied to the speech situation rather than to one animal, and 64 develops it by making the herd's homecoming the very sound that hurts the woman, so the same image both promises his return and measures her waiting.

links.note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for giving the great feast without limit; Akananuru 65 likens the girls' joy at eloping to that of the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral.
links.teaches: The king's puram fame as a feeder of bards had become a proverbial measure of gladness, so an akam friend could express release from a watchful mother by the bards' delight at his court.

links.note: Kural 62 says evil will not touch for seven births those who have children free of blame; Akananuru 66 quotes a saying of the same kind (blameless sons bring fame here and a stainless next world) and finds it true when a toddler stops his father from marrying another wife.
links.teaches: The pair shows a maxim about a child's merit protecting the parent being tested in a household quarrel, where its proof is not the next world but a husband held at home, which shifts the rule from the father's destiny to the mother's marriage.

links.note: Lines 10 and 11 of 67 repeat lines 11 and 12 of 131 word for word (the hero-stones inscribed with names, crowned with peacock feathers, like a battle front with planted spears); in 67 the woman knows the road by report, in 131 the man refuses to take her along it.
links.teaches: The repeated couplet shows the hero-stone road as a fixed formula shared by poets, and the two poems turn it to opposite ends: hearsay that terrifies the woman left at home, and the man's reason for not taking her.

links.note: Both use nearly the same words for the Moriyar, whose chariots under sky-touching umbrellas cut a path through the rock with their wheels: in 69 that rock marks how far the man has gone, in Purananuru 175 the cutting's circle is a likeness for a patron's constancy.
links.teaches: The northern invaders' cut through the hills was a shared memory that akam used as a mark of distance and puram as an image of something fixed and open to all, showing one historical feature serving both kinds of poem.

links.note: Kural 228 asks whether hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Akananuru 69 says the man left for wealth wanting exactly that joy (ஈதல் இன்பம் வெஃகி), and the friend draws from it that he will not delay.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's joy of giving as the stated motive of the akam journey for wealth, so the separation the paalai poems lament is grounded in a virtue, and the friend can use that virtue as a promise of his return.

links.note: Akananuru 70 likens the town's silence after the wedding to the banyan Rama hushed at Kodi for his secret counsel; Purananuru 378 likens a bard's kin, putting on jewels the wrong way, to the monkeys who found Sita's jewels on the ground.
links.teaches: These are two early Tamil uses of the Rama story, both of minor episodes and both as similes, one akam and one puram, which shows the story was familiar enough to be drawn on for a passing likeness rather than told.

links.note: Kural 247 sets wealth and grace side by side as what this world and the next require; the man in Akananuru 75 quotes the saying that effort for wealth, not grace, is a man's task and refuses it, since nothing in this world can give back what parting wastes.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kural's balance of wealth and grace becomes a choice in a marriage, and the akam man qualifies the Kural's grant of this world to wealth by naming one thing in this world that wealth cannot restore.

links.note: In 45 the wife likens herself to Aathi Manthi, distraught after losing her husband; in 76 the courtesan tells the same legend and casts herself as the Kaveri that held the dancer, leaving the wife as Aathi Manthi.
links.teaches: The same legend serves the wife's lament and the courtesan's boast, which shows the akam poets reading a story from either side of a quarrel, and that the river's part could be claimed with pride.

links.note: Purananuru 172 praises Pittan, lord of the hard country, for his spear that wins hard battles and his great giving; Akananuru 77 names Pittan, Chera's warrior with unending toddy, and likens the woman's tearful eyes to the spear he raised against hostile kings.
links.teaches: The pair shows a chief's puram praise (his spear and his gifts) reused in akam, where his famous spear becomes the measure of the pain her eyes will cause, so the poet trusts listeners to know the patron's weapon.

links.note: Purananuru 109 is Kapilar's boast during the siege of Paari's Parambu that the three kings cannot take it by force; Akananuru 78 recalls Paari with Kapilar beside him, holding out for years and driving away the kings with elephants.
links.teaches: The akam poem treats as settled fame what the puram poem speaks in the middle of the siege, so Paari's resistance with Kapilar had become a reference point another poet could use to praise a girl's fragrance.

source_issues: 67: lines 10 and 11 repeat Akananuru 131 lines 11 and 12 word for word (the hero-stone couplet), as the text flag notes; marked as the base text stands.
70: line 9 carries a repaired character (an unassigned code point after ஞ் read as ஞா in ஞாழல்), per the text flag.

71: the colophon says the friend speaks to the heroine, but the poem speaks of என் உயிர் and addresses the friend (வாழி, தோழி), which fits the heroine as speaker; thurai_akam keeps the colophon's speaker.
72: the colophon thurai is numbered (1) but gives no second alternative.

73: the colophon thurai reads as two sentences and names no speaker (தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிகின்றான். குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு அழிந்த தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.); the poem itself addresses காதல்அம் தோழி and speaks of என்அழிபு, which suggests the heroine as speaker. The rain-cloud of the promised season makes the poem mullai on its own evidence, against the colophon's பாலை.
